prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, enabling atomic timekeeping and frequency comparison at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a single, identifiable achievement with a clean causal chain. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the trapping-light shift to first order, which lets many neutral atoms be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime without Doppler or recoil broadening, and Ye's group turned that into the lowest systematic uncertainties and best stability. The result is fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, a credible route to redefining the second, relativistic geodesy, and sensitive searches for varying constants and dark matter. It has been reproduced by many independent laboratories and species (Sr, Yb, Hg) and cross-compared between institutions, so maturity is not in doubt. It also fits the pattern of the field: the comb (2005) and ion-trap (2012) prizes recognised earlier steps in optical frequency metrology, and the neutral-atom lattice clock is the natural next one. Five of eight members rank it in their top five, with three first places, so it is the nearest thing this committee has to a shared view, and the two-name attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap and dilution: Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already covered the comb and single-ion clock, so a reader could see this as an incremental refinement of recognised metrology rather than a new discovery, and the second has not yet been redefined, so the full impact is still pending. Credit within the lattice-clock community is also broader than two names (Takamoto, Ido, Lemonde and others, plus Ye's separate work on combs, cavity-stabilised lasers and the thorium nuclear clock), and I cannot verify the first-demonstration priority from the supplied text. Finally, the broad consensus is only moderate in depth, since several members place it fourth or fifth and none of those who prefer other candidates has yet conceded it is the strongest.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the lattice clock fifth, calls the attribution clean and the timing good, but worries about overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes and puts IceCube neutrino astronomy first.
responses.response: I share the overlap worry and think it is the real test of this candidate, but I do not think it is decisive. The 2005 prize covered the comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize covered control of single quantum systems; neither covered a many-atom, light-shift-cancelled lattice that moves the whole field to 1e-18. That is a new principle, not a refinement of an old one. I take IceCube seriously as a discovery of nature and accept it is a strong alternative, but its source identification is partial by your own account and the attribution has to handle AMANDA, Baikal and the larger collaboration. I would prefer the case where both attribution and maturity are settled.

responses.point: Johansson puts circuit QED first and trapped ions and cold atoms second, ranks the clocks fourth, and notes that the thorium nuclear clock candidate could dilute Ye's claim.
responses.response: I agree circuit QED is a lasting idea, but the four-name credit forces leaving out one of Blais or Girvin, which you acknowledge is a real allocation problem, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits sits very close. On Ye and thorium, I would credit him strictly for the strontium lattice clock and its record comparisons, and keep the nuclear clock out of the citation; that is still a nascent programme, not part of this achievement. I would support B053 as the fallback, since you rank it second, but there the experimental credit is shared across several ion groups.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery first on the grounds that it is decisive and that the 2013 prize covered only theory, and he does not place lattice clocks in his top eight.
responses.response: The discovery is certainly decisive, and I do not question its scientific weight. My reservation is attribution: naming Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee is a proxy for leadership of two collaborations of thousands, and Lindroth makes the same point. A prize that cannot say who did the discovery risks being arbitrary, whereas for the lattice clock the proposer and the group that realised the record performance are individually identifiable. If the committee is willing to accept leadership credit, I would want to hear which analysis or detector contributions justify these three names rather than spokespersons or analysis leaders.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first, stresses the Lamb-Dicke regime and the 1e-18 level, and says the timing is right with the redefinition of the second under discussion.
responses.response: I agree on the physics and the maturity. Where I would add a qualification to our shared view is on timing: since the second has not yet been redefined, we should not let the redefinition drive the citation. The citation should rest on what has been demonstrated, namely lattice clocks at 1e-18 and the inter-laboratory comparisons, so that the award stands on its own whatever the metrology bodies decide.

uncertainties: Whether Takamoto, Ido or Lemonde have a first-demonstration claim that the two-name credit does not cover.
How to word the citation so that Ye is credited for the lattice clock and not for the comb or nuclear-clock work.
Whether the committee regards neutral-atom lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether a pending redefinition of the second should affect timing.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder; Hall's 2005 recognition is adjacent to this field and Ye works in the same optical-frequency-metrology tradition, so I flag that connection for the chair's judgement, although the profile does not document any personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye. I also have documented ties to Lund colleagues, WACQT and Deep Light Vision; these bear on quantum-memory and quantum-computing candidates such as B053 more than on B042, and I would flag them if the discussion moves toward those candidates.
